name: Whey/creatine bulking for neck

lead: Looksmaxxers combine neck training with a calorie surplus, whey protein and creatine monohydrate to build a thicker neck, which they say gives the jaw and frame a stronger look.

Creatine raises muscle phosphocreatine stores and is reported to support high-intensity training capacity and, with resistance training, lean mass; early weight gain is largely water held in muscle. Protein supplements provide dietary protein for muscle repair. These findings concern skeletal muscle in general, and no human study has measured effects on neck size specifically.

paras: People eat in a calorie surplus, take whey and creatine daily, and train the neck directly with resistance a few times per week. Muscle gain builds over months, with creatine's early scale-weight rise mostly water.

A position stand cited on Wikipedia describes creatine as safe for healthy people, and a National Kidney Foundation review found creatinine rises within normal limits. Safety data are lacking for children and pregnancy, and supplement contamination has been reported in some surveys.

web.title: My Neck, My Back (Lick It) — Wikipedia

angle.text: A calorie surplus with whey and creatine supports the muscle gain from direct neck exercises, which adds neck size and a stronger-looking frame and jaw area. Creatine and protein are among the most studied muscle-building supplements, though not for the neck specifically.

lead: Whey and creatine bulking for the neck is the practice of pairing a calorie surplus, whey protein powder and creatine monohydrate with direct neck exercises to build a thicker neck. A larger neck is discussed in looksmaxxing communities as a way to give the frame a more powerful look, to balance wide shoulders and to make the jaw and head appear better supported. The supplements are used so that neck training has enough protein, energy and training capacity behind it.

Creatine is among the most studied sports supplements. Reviews report that it improves performance in short, high-intensity exercise and, combined with resistance training, can increase lean mass.[1] Whey is a milk protein sold in concentrate, isolate and hydrolysate forms and used mainly for muscle growth and recovery.[2] A meta-analysis of 49 trials with 1,863 participants found that protein supplementation added modest gains in strength and fat-free mass during prolonged resistance training, with larger gains in resistance-trained people.[3]

These findings concern skeletal muscle in general. No published human study has measured the effect of whey or creatine on neck circumference, so the neck application rests on the assumption that neck muscles respond like other trained muscles.
infobox: Calorie surplus, whey protein, creatine monohydrate, neck exercises

paras: The practice combines three elements discussed on forums: eating above maintenance calories, taking supplemental protein such as whey, and taking creatine monohydrate, alongside neck-specific resistance work. Practitioners describe the neck as a muscle group that responds to training like other muscles.

On looksmax.org, whey is discussed alongside casein. One thread argues that whey suits the period after a workout because it digests quickly, while slow-digesting casein suits other times and before bed, and says dairy proteins raise IGF-1; the poster also says frequent whey causes bloating.[4]

Creatine is an organic compound that helps regenerate ATP, with about 95 percent of the body's stores in skeletal muscle. Supplementation is reported to raise muscle phosphocreatine by roughly 20 to 40 percent and to improve repeated high-intensity work, with no significant effect on aerobic endurance.[1]

A 2018 review in the Journal of the International Society of Sports Nutrition described creatine monohydrate as the most effective supplement for increasing high-intensity exercise capacity and muscle mass during training.[1] Early weight gain, usually in the first week, is mainly water retained in muscle.[1]

Whey protein is made from the liquid left after milk is coagulated for cheese; its main proteins are beta-lactoglobulin and alpha-lactalbumin. The Wikipedia article reports that a 2010 European Food Safety Authority panel judged whey roughly as effective as other protein sources for building strength, muscle and lean mass.[2] A randomised trial found no significant difference in muscle growth or strength between soy and whey protein matched for leucine over 12 weeks of resistance training.[5]

A randomised controlled trial in Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise examined whey isolate and creatine monohydrate, separately and together, with resistance training on body composition, strength and muscle fibre hypertrophy.[6]

A position stand summarised on Wikipedia describes creatine as safe for healthy people, and a 2019 National Kidney Foundation review of 15 studies found creatinine levels that rose slightly but stayed within normal limits; three case reports described possible renal effects.[1] Safety data are lacking for children and pregnancy.[1] A 2011 survey of 33 Italian supplements found over half exceeded European limits for at least one contaminant.[1]

A systematic review of 11 papers on whey reported that most documented adverse effects were linked to chronic, high-volume use, with kidneys and liver the main organs mentioned, plus acne and microbiota changes.[7] A dermatology review lists whey among dietary supplements linked to acne, typically papulonodular lesions on the trunk and sometimes the face, which generally resolve after stopping.[8]

No studies found on whey or creatine for neck size or neck appearance. Trials in other populations measured muscle mass and strength generally: the 49-trial protein meta-analysis,[3] the whey isolate and creatine hypertrophy trial,[6] and the soy versus whey trial.[5]

lore.intro: Supplement choice for muscle building, including whey versus casein, is a recurring topic on looksmax.org, though neck-specific supplement material is thin.[4]
